name: Wellington
title: Wellington Ship Gauging: UTM for Cook Strait Ferries and Tankers
description: Ultrasonic thickness gauging in Wellington for Cook Strait ferries, product tankers, container ships and log carriers: car decks, tanks, hull and piping.
h1: Thickness Measurement for Ferries, Tankers and Cargo Ships in Wellington
intro: Wellington, New Zealand's capital, sits on a deep harbour at the southern tip of the North Island, where the Cook Strait ferries link the road and rail networks of the two islands and product tankers bring in fuel for much of the lower North Island. Container ships, log carriers, car carriers and cruise ships complete the traffic. Gauging is done alongside or during ferry lay-overs and refits, by technicians who travel from India to the vessel each time; Atlantis has no staff in the country.

highlights.h: Ferries on the Cook Strait crossing
highlights.p: Interislander and Bluebridge ro-ro ferries cross Cook Strait several times a day with trucks, cars, passengers and, on the rail-enabled ships, rail wagons, through some of the roughest water on the coast. Car deck plating, ramps, bow and stern door structure and ballast tanks wear quickly and suit a regular gauging programme.

Product tankers discharge at the Seaview wharf in Lower Hutt, the main fuel entry point for the lower North Island, and at Burnham Wharf in Evans Bay for aviation fuel. Ballast tanks, deck structure and cargo piping on these tankers can be measured within the terminal's permit system.

highlights.h: Wind, swell and a narrow entrance
highlights.p: The harbour entrance is narrow and exposed to southerly gales funnelling through Cook Strait. Ships sometimes hold off or delay sailing, and launch work is often impossible, so jobs are planned alongside, as a ranked list of spaces matched to the berth time the agent confirms.

port.h: Wellington Harbour, Cook Strait weather and CentrePort's berths
p: Wellington Harbour, Te Whanganui-a-Tara, is a large, deep and almost enclosed basin reached from Cook Strait through a narrow entrance beside Pencarrow Head. Cook Strait funnels the prevailing north-westerlies and the cold southerly fronts between the two islands, and the city is known as one of the windiest anywhere, conditions that have shaped seamanship here since the inter-island ferry Wahine was lost at the harbour entrance in a storm in 1968. Pilotage is compulsory for larger ships. Inside, the water is sheltered and deep, and the commercial wharves lie along the western shore close to the city centre, with the main fuel wharf at Seaview on the eastern shore near Lower Hutt and an aviation fuel wharf in Evans Bay serving the airport.

CentrePort operates the commercial port. The Thorndon container wharf, repaired, strengthened and lengthened after the 2016 Kaikōura earthquake, receives deep-sea and coastal container services, while Aotea Quay handles logs, vehicles, ro-ro cargo, steel and cement and berths many of the cruise ships that call through the summer. The two Cook Strait ferry operators, KiwiRail's Interislander and StraitNZ's Bluebridge, run several return crossings a day to Picton from their terminals at the northern end of the port, and the regional council has chosen Kaiwharawhara as the site for a single terminal to serve both. Product tankers supply petrol, diesel and jet fuel, a bunker tanker serves ships at the berths, and the harbour is home to tugs, pilot launches, fishing vessels and research vessels. Logs are trucked and railed in from forests across the lower North Island and stored on the port and at an inland depot in the Wairarapa.

Stays are short and regular. The ferries turn round at their berths between crossings and lay over at night, while container ships and car carriers spend roughly a day alongside and log carriers stay longer while their stows are built. The tidal range is small, so tides seldom affect access, but the wind does: southerly storms can stop cargo work, suspend some harbour movements and make boarding by launch unsafe. Ferries are taken out of service in turn for their refits and surveys, scheduled away from the busiest holiday periods, and those refit periods, together with the night lay-overs, are when the most thorough gauging can be done on them. Cruise calls concentrate between late spring and early autumn. Log loading in particular pauses in very strong wind, which can extend a log carrier's stay by a day or more.

All Wellington gauging is done afloat. On the ferries, the team works car and rail decks, ramp and door structure, void spaces and ballast tanks during night lay-overs at the terminal berths or during a refit period, when the ship is out of service and spaces can be opened in sequence. At the Thorndon container wharf and Aotea Quay, container ships, log carriers and car carriers are measured during cargo work, keeping clear of crane lanes, log loaders and driving routes. Tankers at Seaview are gauged under the terminal's permits, normally limited to deck, ballast tanks and piping while cargo is being discharged. Ships at anchor are rarely a practical option given the harbour weather.

Wellington has no dry dock today. Its floating dock left the harbour in the late 1980s, and the historic patent slip in Evans Bay no longer hauls out ships. Pilot launches, workboats and fishing boats are lifted out at local boatyards and slipways, but a ferry or merchant ship needing a docking goes elsewhere: to Auckland's Calliope Dock or Lyttelton's dry dock if it fits, or overseas. That makes a Wellington lay-over the place to measure steel and prepare the docking specification, so the yard has a renewal list before the ship arrives.
list: Interislander and Bluebridge ferry berths — car and rail decks, ramps, doors and ballast tanks during night lay-overs
Thorndon container wharf — deck plating, hatch coamings and tanks on container ships during the exchange
Aotea Quay — log carriers, car carriers, ro-ro and general cargo ships, and summer cruise calls
Seaview wharf, Lower Hutt — product tankers discharging under the terminal's permit system
Burnham Wharf, Evans Bay — tankers discharging aviation fuel for the airport
Local boatyards and slipways — pilot launches, workboats and fishing boats out of the water

context.h: Maritime New Zealand, ferry safety and the fuel trade
p: Maritime New Zealand inspects foreign-flagged ships at Wellington under the Tokyo MoU, and as the national maritime regulator, headquartered in the capital, it also oversees the domestic ferry services under New Zealand's own maritime rules. The Cook Strait ferries have drawn close public and regulatory attention in recent years, after mechanical breakdowns, a grounding near Picton in 2024 and the cancellation of a planned replacement ferry project, so operators need clear evidence that the ships they keep running are structurally sound. A measured record of car deck, ramp, shell and tank condition supports both the statutory survey and the operator's own maintenance planning, and shows where steel work is needed before it becomes urgent.

Fuel adds its own demands. Seaview is the main fuel connection for the lower North Island, and the tankers serving it, many on regular coastal or trans-Tasman runs since New Zealand stopped refining crude oil in 2022, load and discharge often, so ballast tanks and cargo piping work through frequent cycles. Short, rough passages across Cook Strait and along the coast load ferries and coastal ships differently from deep-sea ships: slamming in head seas works the bow structure and forward ballast tanks, wave loads strain ramp and door hinges, and heavy vehicles running on and off several times a day wear car deck plating and its supporting stiffeners. Gauging those areas on a regular programme, rather than only at the renewal survey, gives operators warning of wastage before it turns into a repair emergency.

jobs.h: Gauging jobs we see at Wellington
jobs.p: Wellington work divides between the ferry operators and the visiting cargo ships. Ferry jobs are planned with the operator's technical team around the timetable, using night lay-overs for short, focused scopes and refit periods for full programmes, and the readings feed both the survey and the operator's repair planning. Cargo ship jobs follow the familiar owner pattern of condition gauging, pre-docking steel estimates and pre-purchase inspections fitted into a day or two alongside, while tanker work is shaped by the Seaview terminal's rules. In every case the TM plan is drawn up from the ship's own drawings before the team travels, and the scope is ranked so that the items driving repair decisions are measured first if the weather or the schedule shortens the job.
list: Car deck, ramp and ballast tank gauging on a Cook Strait ro-ro ferry spread across a sequence of night lay-overs at its terminal berth.
Full hull and tank gauging on a ferry during its refit period, building the steel renewal list for its next docking.
Owner's condition gauging of a product tanker's ballast tanks, deck and cargo piping during discharge at Seaview.
Hold and hatch coaming gauging on a log carrier at Aotea Quay before loading starts, with magnetic particle crack detection at coaming corners.
Pre-purchase inspection of a coastal container ship or general cargo ship alongside at Thorndon or Aotea Quay.

logistics: Wellington International Airport sits on the Rongotai isthmus close to the port, with domestic flights and services to Australia and the Pacific; from India the team usually arrives through Auckland or an Australian hub and connects onward. Indian passport holders need a New Zealand visa that allows short-term specialist work, applied for as soon as the job is firm and supported by a letter from the owner or operator; processing times vary. CentrePort inductions, terminal access and escorts are arranged by the ship's agent or the ferry operator.
vessels: Cook Strait ro-ro passenger and rail ferries
Car carriers and ro-ro cargo ships
Tugs, pilot launches and research vessels

faqs.q: Can a Cook Strait ferry be gauged without taking it out of service?
faqs.a: Partly. Night lay-overs at the terminal berth give a few hours each night for focused work on car decks, ramps, voids and selected ballast tanks, and a scope can be spread across several nights. A full programme covering the hull, all tanks and the main structure is better done during the ferry's refit period, when spaces can be opened and ventilated in sequence without timetable pressure.

faqs.q: Is there anywhere in Wellington to dry-dock a ship?
faqs.a: No. The floating dock that once served the harbour left in the late 1980s, and the old Evans Bay slip no longer hauls out ships. Small craft can be lifted at local boatyards, but ferries and merchant ships dock in Auckland, Lyttelton or overseas, depending on their size. We often gauge here first so the docking yard receives a steel list in advance.

faqs.q: How does the weather affect inspection work in Wellington?
faqs.a: Strong winds, especially southerly storms, can stop cargo work, delay sailings and make launch transfers unsafe, so we plan work alongside rather than at anchor. Wind rarely stops work inside tanks once the ship is safely moored, but deck and external work may pause. A ranked scope and some spare time in the plan protect the most important readings when the weather intervenes.

faqs.q: Can tankers be gauged while discharging at Seaview?
faqs.a: Some of the work, yes. Ballast tanks, the deck, void spaces and cargo piping outside the hazardous zones can usually be measured during discharge, within the terminal's permit rules on equipment and ignition sources near cargo vapour. Cargo tanks need cleaning, gas-freeing and an entry certificate, which is more practical at a lay-by berth or during a docking than at a working fuel terminal.
